# The American Transfer {#sec-1-09}

::: {.chapter-meta}
The World Before California · 1788–1848
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does a continent change hands on paper?

**The answer.** By war debt, by a penal colony that learns to trade, and by a
treaty signed in ignorance of gold. The American title to the West is not a
destiny. It is a sequence of European emergencies.

**The mechanism.** Public subsidy converted into private monopoly, at continental
scale: Napoleon's treasury, Britain's Pacific labour system, Polk's war, a
border drawn in Mexico City.

**The key fact.** The Louisiana Purchase is the land *west* of the Mississippi,
sold in 1803 to fund Napoleon's wars. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, 2
February 1848, transfers California nine days after Marshall finds gold, and
nobody in the room knows.

**The human anchor.** Napoleon ordering mourning for Washington — two republics
recognising each other — and then selling a third of a continent to pay for the
next war.

**Excluded voices.** The nations already living on every acre that changed
hands.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that the American West arrives as a European
liquidation by showing the debts and treaties that moved the title.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

Britain plants a penal colony at Sydney in 1788; the colony becomes a going
concern and trades into the Pacific, including with China, on its own account.
Napoleon, First Consul, mourns Washington and then sells Louisiana to Jefferson
to fund wars he cannot stop fighting. The purchase is the drainage of the
Mississippi — west of the river, not east. Polk fights Mexico; the Treaty of
Guadalupe Hidalgo moves the border. Spain had held the same coast with missions
and presidios. The companion volume begins on the street named for the man who
ordered those missions built.
:::

:::

::: {.chapter-question}
How does a continent change hands on paper?
:::

George Washington died on the fourteenth of December, 1799. Napoleon Bonaparte,
First Consul of the French Republic, ordered ten days of mourning. The gesture
is easy to sentimentalise and more useful if you do not. Two revolutionary
states, still young, recognised each other as the same kind of experiment — and
the one that was about to go back to war was already looking for something it
could sell.

## A colony that learned to trade

In 1788 Britain landed a convict fleet at Port Jackson. The official purpose was
disposal: prisoners and debtors, a labour system at the other end of the earth,
cheap because the land was treated as empty. The unofficial result, within a
generation, was a Pacific economy. Wool, then gold, then ships that did not need
London's permission for every hold they filled. Australian merchants traded into
China on their own account, which is a small sentence about a large fact:
empires plant labour systems, and the systems become markets that outgrow the
planters.

The same ocean washed California. The same China trade that enriched Sydney and
Boston would, a lifetime later, make a railroad across the American West look
like a necessity rather than a speculation.

## What Napoleon actually sold

In 1803 Jefferson's government bought from France the drainage of the
Mississippi — the land *west* of the river, not east of it. The east bank was
already American. What changed hands was a claim, poorly mapped, over an
interior France could no longer afford to hold after the loss of Saint-Domingue
and under the cost of a European war that had no obvious end.

The purchase is usually told as Jefferson's vision. It is also Napoleon's
treasury. A state drowning in war debt liquidates a continent it cannot garrison
and calls the sale strategy. The pattern is older than either man. *Dawn* has
been watching it since the palaces burned.

## The second paper border

Half a century later the United States fought Mexico and wrote a new line at
Guadalupe Hidalgo, on the second of February, 1848. James K. Polk wanted a
Pacific port. Spain had already tried to hold that coast with a chain of
missions and presidios — an administrative idea conceived in Mexico City by José
de Gálvez, executed by a Franciscan named Serra, and still posted, a century on,
as a street sign at the front of a California university. Mexico had inherited
the claim and not the capacity. The treaty moved the title anyway.

Nine days earlier, at Sutter's Mill, a carpenter had found gold. The negotiators
did not know. Washington did not know. The most valuable real estate on the
continent changed hands at a price set in ignorance.

That is the end of this book and the start of the other one. The old world spent
three thousand years learning how to turn a passage into a title and a title
into a class. California runs the same machine in one place, in one lifetime,
with the documents still on the ground.

The walk begins on Galvez Street.
